mcqs.question: A week after a mobile release, a backend engineer assumes traffic is now entirely from the new client version. Why is this assumption usually wrong?
options: There's no way to force every installed app onto the new version, so the backend keeps serving a mix of many client versions, often spanning years, indefinitely
App stores automatically force-update all devices within 24 hours
It's actually correct — mobile releases behave identically to backend deploys
Only devices with automatic updates disabled continue running old versions
mcqs.explanation: Unlike a backend deploy where the old version disappears within minutes, mobile has no mechanism to force every device onto the latest release — a meaningful fraction of traffic can still come from versions a year or more old, indefinitely, not just from users with auto-update disabled.

mcqs.question: A team runs a staged rollout to 1%, then 10%, then 50%, then 100%, but never checks any metrics in between stages, just advancing on a fixed schedule. What protection does this staged rollout actually provide?
options: Full protection — the percentage staging alone prevents any bad release from reaching all users
None of the intended protection — staging without watching a real signal at each stage means a regression can sail through every stage undetected before reaching 100%
Protection only against crashes, not against other regressions
The same protection as a kill switch would provide
mcqs.explanation: A staged rollout only protects users if a real-time signal is actually monitored and a pause threshold is enforced at each stage — advancing on a fixed schedule regardless of metrics provides none of the intended safety net, since a regression at 1% would simply continue widening unnoticed.

mcqs.question: Why does shipping a risky new feature behind a remote flag, defaulted off, in the same release as everything else matter?
options: It reduces the app's binary size compared to a separate release
It decouples code being released from the feature being active — if something's wrong, the flag can be flipped off instantly without waiting for a new release to clear store review
It's required by app store policy for all new features
It eliminates the need for staged rollouts entirely
mcqs.explanation: A flag-gated feature can be disabled in seconds server-side regardless of what version is installed, while a broken feature with no flag requires a full release cycle including store review to fix — flags don't replace staged rollouts, they complement them as a faster mitigation path.

mcqs.question: Why can't a backend team simply remove a field from an API response once the mobile team has released an update that stops needing it?
options: Removing fields from API responses is technically impossible
Because clients running versions older than that update are still calling the API and reading that field, and they have no way to be forced onto the newer version
Field removal is only disallowed on weekends per most companies' deploy policies
Because the app store requires all fields to remain permanently in the API contract
mcqs.explanation: Old client versions that predate the update continue calling the same API indefinitely with no way to force them to upgrade, so removing a field they still parse breaks them — the safe pattern is deprecating in place and using real client-version telemetry to decide when a field is truly safe to retire.

mcqs.question: A backend team changes an API response field's format a week after the mobile app update that handles the new format was released, reasoning enough time has passed. What's the flaw in that reasoning?
options: Mobile release and mobile adoption are decoupled by weeks or months, and adoption of any single version never reaches 100%, so old clients are still calling the API and will break
The reasoning is sound; a week is generally sufficient for mobile updates to fully propagate
The flaw is only that a week is too short — a month would have been safe
API response formats cannot actually be changed once released, regardless of timing
mcqs.explanation: Unlike backend deploys where release and full adoption happen together, mobile adoption trails release by weeks to months and never reaches 100% for any version, since some users are permanently stuck on old OS versions or devices — no waiting period alone makes an unversioned breaking change safe.

mcqs.question: A team's entire backward-compatibility strategy is a forced-update screen that blocks usage below a minimum app version. What's the gap in this approach?
options: Forced updates are against app store policy and will get the app rejected
It fully solves compatibility, since every user can simply update to the latest version
It works, but only for users on iOS, not Android
Users who can't update — due to an unsupported OS version, poor connectivity, or infrequent app usage — are locked out entirely, turning a compatibility problem into a support and churn problem
mcqs.explanation: A forced update only helps users who are actually able to update; those who can't for device, connectivity, or usage-pattern reasons are simply locked out, often mid-task — forced updates are a reasonable last resort for genuine emergencies, not a substitute for designing graceful backward compatibility.
